tEn: Spatial Design Experiments: Making Ideas Feel Real
tZh: 空间设计实验：让想法变得真实
sEn: Microsoft designer Ryan Steven shares how he creates striking spatial design experiments using tools like After Effects and Blender to bring futuristic ideas to life.
sZh: 微软设计师 Ryan Steven 分享如何利用 After Effects 和 Blender 等工具打造令人惊艳的空间设计实验，将未来概念变为现实。

consensus.en: Making ideas feel real is the designer's core opportunity, choosing film, code, or simple tools as needed.
consensus.zh: 让想法变得真实是设计师的核心机会，可在影视、代码或简单工具中任选。

consensus.en: Keeping a running list of playful, exaggerated ideas and sketching frequently fuels creative output.
consensus.zh: 保持一份俏皮、夸张的想法清单并频繁画草图，能激发源源不断的创意。

consensus.en: Prototyping is effective for testing ideas, persuading leadership, and running research studies.
consensus.zh: 原型制作是检验想法、说服领导层和开展研究的高效方式。

consensus.en: Sharing work publicly has low downside and high upside; you always learn something.
consensus.zh: 公开发布作品风险低、回报高；即使失败也能学到东西。

consensus.en: Visibility is a powerful currency, both on social media and inside an organization.
consensus.zh: 可见度是很有价值的货币，无论在社交媒体还是在组织内部。

consensus.en: Effort fidelity matters more than visual fidelity; only make the essential aspects feel real.
consensus.zh: 努力保真度比视觉保真度更重要；只需把核心面向做真实。

contrarian.en: Spatial design doesn't require heavy tools; low-fi phone videos with drawn overlays can work.
contrarian.zh: 空间设计不一定要用重型工具；手机拍的视频加手绘覆盖层就够。

contrarian.en: Tools should inform ideas as much as ideas inform tools; let the medium shape the outcome.
contrarian.zh: 工具应当与想法相互影响；让媒介反过来塑造结果。

contrarian.en: High-fidelity prototypes early can yield clearer feedback than low-fidelity concepts.
contrarian.zh: 早期就给出高保真原型，能比低保真概念得到更明确的反馈。

contrarian.en: Use the crazy eights method backwards—sketch metaphors and observations, not solutions.
contrarian.zh: 反向使用“疯狂八格法”——画隐喻与观察，而不是解决方案。

contrarian.en: Fat-marker sketches intentionally prevent detail, forcing focus on core interaction.
contrarian.zh: 粗头笔草图有意避免细节，迫使你聚焦核心交互。

contrarian.en: A playful, non-functional idea can communicate powerfully without being practical.
contrarian.zh: 一个俏皮、非功能性的想法，即使不实用也能有力传达。

turns.en: It reminds me of something my friend Gabe Valdivia said, probably a long time ago at this point on the show, where he talked about how the best designers are almost content creators within their org. And everything you're saying, I'm just nodding along. That makes sense. You are asking for people's attention. It's not a given that you're going to get it. You have to do something that is compelling and interesting or makes people stop and be like, “Huh, didn't think about it that way.”
turns.zh: 这让我想起我的朋友 Gabe Valdivia 的话，可能是很久以前在节目里说的。他谈到最优秀的设计师几乎就是组织内部的内容创作者。你说的每一点我都在点头，确实有道理。你是在争夺人们的注意力，这不是理所当然的事。你必须做一些有说服力、有趣的事，或者让人们停下来想：“嗯，原来还可以这样想。”

turns.en: Yeah, I think also we work increasingly on global experiences and collaborations, right? So if I can send you an async video that tells a story and uses a lot of these same techniques that we looked at today, what an impactful career thing to not need a synchronous 30-minute meeting to maybe walk through part of your thing. For me, it's like, how do we tell an idea without getting lost in the tool shed? You know, there are more tools today than ever before. So how do we tell a story and go from there?
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得我们也越来越多地在做全球化的体验和协作，对吧？所以如果我能给你发一个异步视频，用它来讲一个故事，并且用上我们今天看到的这些技巧，那是一件很有影响力的事：不需要一个同步的 30 分钟会议来走一遍你想讲的东西。对我来说，问题是我们如何讲清楚一个想法，而不迷失在工具堆里？如今工具比以往任何时候都多，那么我们如何讲一个故事，然后继续推进？

turns.en: As somebody who's been kind of putting the reps in on storytelling, potentially even internally and externally, are you able to look back on your last few years and see clear areas where you've grown as a storyteller, or potentially lessons that you've learned or techniques that you've adopted over time?
turns.zh: 作为一位在讲故事上不断下功夫的人，可能对内对外都在练，你能不能回顾一下过去几年，看到自己在讲故事方面有哪些明显的成长，或者学到了什么教训，又或者逐渐采用了哪些技巧？

turns.en: I think the biggest one has been being able to tailor the story to who I'm talking to as the audience. Obviously, we've talked a lot today about very iteratively getting better at telling these bite-sized stories online, but internally too, I think how you tell a story when you're wanting feedback from a design team is super different from the type of story you would tell to a leader that may not be in the weeds as much. I think prototypes are an awesome way to move out of all the context setting sometimes, and move out of ten slides of explaining what the perfect thing is, and really letting someone just evaluate the thing, which is what matters at the end of the day.
turns.zh: 我觉得最大的收获是能够根据听众来调整故事。显然我们今天聊了很多关于如何迭代式地提升这类短小精悍的在线故事的讲述，但在内部也一样。当你希望从设计团队那里获得反馈时，你讲故事的方式，和你讲给一位可能不那么深入细节的领导者听，是非常不同的。我认为原型是一种很棒的方式，有时可以跳出所有背景铺垫，也跳出十页幻灯片去解释那个完美的东西是什么，而是直接让某人评估那个东西，而这才是一天结束时真正重要的。

turns.en: Yeah. Something I think a lot about is—I don't know, for years I had this idea presented to me from so many different designers—which is you have to reduce the fidelity as long as possible so you can make sure that you're aligned before getting lost in the details. And there's this fear that if I show too much detail, I'll get bad feedback. And I have had that happen before, for sure. I've lost control because people are obsessing over a little UI piece, and that's not the reason that we're here. That being said, the flip side I almost never hear people talk about is if you keep the fidelity low, people can just nod along in agreement because they totally agree with all the high-level stuff. And then you get to the point where you're like, “Okay, here it is.” And then they look at it and it's like, “Oh, that wasn't what I had in my head at all.” And you almost assume that the details will get fleshed out when we increase the fidelity. But it's like, yeah, there's still a pretty large execution gap there. And the longer that we push that off... I've run into that issue many times where I've felt the pain of keeping the fidelity low. Whereas if you show somebody a really slick prototype right out of the gate, they're going to know if they like it or not. They're going to be able to point to it very specifically and say, “No, I don't like this part.” Or, “Yeah, that makes sense.”
turns.zh: 是的。我经常在想的一个问题是——我不知道，多年来有好多不同的设计师跟我讲过一个观点：你必须在尽可能长的时间里降低保真度，这样才能确保在对齐之后再陷入细节。还有这种恐惧：如果我展示了太多细节，会得到不好的反馈。我当然也遇到过这种情况，我确实失去过控制，因为人们纠结于一个小小的界面细节，而那不是我们在这里的原因。话虽如此，我几乎没听人谈过另一面：如果你一直保持低保真度，人们可能只是点头同意，因为他们完全赞同所有高层的概念。然后等到你说“好了，就是这样”的时候，他们看了一眼说“噢，这和我脑子里想的完全不一样”。你几乎会认为，等到提高保真度的时候，细节自然会被填补。但问题是，那里仍然有一个相当大的执行差距。而且我们越拖……我遇到过很多次这种问题，我能感受到低保真度的痛苦。反过来，如果你一开始就给某人看一个非常流畅的原型，他们会立刻知道自己喜不喜欢。他们会非常具体地指出来：“不，我不喜欢这部分”或者“对，这讲得通”。

turns.en: Yeah. What I like to think about is effort fidelity more than visual fidelity. So if I can make something in a day or a weekend or a week internally or externally, that fidelity is what matters, not necessarily how awesome the rectangles move around the screen.
turns.zh: 是的。我喜欢考虑的是“努力保真度”（effort fidelity），而不是视觉保真度。所以如果我能用一天、一个周末或一周的内部或外部时间做出来，那个保真度才是重要的，而不一定是矩形在屏幕上移动得多漂亮。

turns.en: And that's so important too with the tools, because it used to be a lot more clear in terms of the correlation between fidelity and time. It's like, yeah, of course it's going to take you more time to make the high fidelity thing, but now it's like actually nobody knows anymore. You could make something incredibly high fidelity in one good prompt. And that kind of changes the equation a little bit.
turns.zh: 这一点在工具方面也非常重要，因为过去保真度和时间之间的关联更明确。就是说，是的，做高保真的东西当然需要更多时间，但现在其实没人知道了。你用一个好的提示词就能做出难以置信的高保真作品。这有点改变了这个等式。

turns.en: And I think also, as designers, we have a role. If we're making ideas feel real, what aspect of the idea needs to feel real? Do the visuals need to feel real? Does this gesture need to feel really real? Does this information architecture need to feel real? Maybe the actual only thing that needs to be real is the language you're using on the screen.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得作为设计师，我们的角色是：如果我们要让想法变得真实，那么这个想法的哪一部分需要变得真实？视觉需要真实吗？这个手势需要非常真实吗？这个信息架构需要真实吗？也许唯一需要真实的就是你在屏幕上使用的语言。

turns.en: Yeah, it might just be like a data thing.
turns.zh: 是的，可能只是数据层面的事。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, exactly. So I think that's also something to think critically on, and something I'm challenging myself every day. I'll make something and kind of play my own feedback loop of, hey, was this real in the right way?
turns.zh: 对对，完全正确。所以我觉得这也值得批判性地思考，而且是我每天都在挑战自己的事：我会做出一些东西，然后跟自己玩一个反馈循环：嘿，这东西用正确的方式真实了吗？

turns.en: Well, Ryan, I appreciate you coming on and giving us a little tour of your work and helping us get inside of your brain and just how you ideate and your process for creativity. Everything in that bucket has been really fascinating, and you have one of the more interesting bodies of work of any designer that I've met. I appreciate you for it. So thanks for coming on today and sharing it with us.
turns.zh: 好的，Ryan，感谢你来做客，带我们参观了一下你的作品，让我们了解你的思维方式、你的创意流程。这些东西都非常迷人。在所有我见过的设计师里，你的作品集是相当有趣的一组。我很感激你，所以谢谢你今天来和我们分享。

turns.en: Before I let you go, I want to take just one minute to run you through my favorite products, because I'm constantly asked what's in my stack. Framer is how I build websites. Genway is how I do research. Granola is how I take notes during crit. Jitter is how I animate my designs. Lovable is how I build my ideas in code. Mobbin is how I find design inspiration. Paper is how I design like a creative. And Raycast is my shortcut every step of the way. Now, I've hand-selected these companies so that I can do these episodes full-time. So by far the number one way to support the show is to check them out. You can find the full list at dive.club/partners.
turns.zh: 在你走之前，我想花一分钟介绍一下我最喜欢的产品，因为总有人问我的工具栈。Framer 是我建网站的工具，Genway 是我做研究的工具，Granola 是我在设计评审会上记笔记的工具，Jitter 是我给设计做动画的工具，Lovable 是我用代码实现想法的工具，Mobbin 是我寻找设计灵感的地方，Paper 是我像创意人一样设计的工具，而 Raycast 是我一路上的快捷键。我精挑细选了这些公司，这样我才能全职做这些节目。所以目前支持这个节目最重要的方式就是去看看它们。你可以在 dive.club/partners 找到完整列表。
